subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Meeting: Read-Aloud and Choral Recitation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Recite (p.103): read aloud and choral recitation of the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads 'The Swing' (p.103) expressively while students follow along in their textbooks. A second reading invites students to listen for the rhythm and the feeling of movement the poem creates.

Let us Recite (p.103) — whole-class choral recitation, stanza by stanza. Teacher models the rise and fall of voice to match the swing's motion; students repeat each stanza together until the reading feels natural and rhythmic.

Paired practice: each pair takes turns reading the poem aloud to each other, alternating stanzas. Teacher moves through the class, offering a quick word of encouragement and correcting pronunciation of 'pleasantest' and 'countryside'.
Three volunteers recite the full poem from memory (or near-memory) for the class. The class offers a brief appreciation — one thing they noticed about how the poem sounded.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's ABAB rhyme and the recurring phrase 'Up in the air' give it a strong oral rhythm — lean into that rhythm during choral reading so students feel the swing-like back-and-forth. 'Pleasantest' (a superlative) and 'countryside' are the two words likely to trip up pronunciation; model them slowly before the choral round.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem: New Words and Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: New Words (p.103): read and understand pleasantest, cattle, countryside.
Let us Think A (p.104): discuss what the poet sees, which lines show enjoyment, and why the air is called blue.

time_bands.activity: Quick choral re-reading of the full poem (p.103). Teacher then writes 'pleasantest', 'cattle', and 'countryside' on the board and elicits guesses about their meanings from context before confirming them.

New Words (p.103) — teacher works through each word with a simple definition and a gesture or quick sketch: 'cattle' (draw a cow outline), 'countryside' (sweep the hand wide), 'pleasantest' (biggest-smile mime). Students repeat each word and say a sentence using it.

Let us Think A (p.104) — teacher poses each question to the class and invites two or three responses before offering a model answer. Question 1 focuses on the second stanza's landscape: rivers, trees, cattle, countryside. Question 2 asks students to locate the lines 'Oh, I do think it the pleasantest thing / Ever a child can do!' to confirm enjoyment. Question 3 opens a short imaginative discussion about the blue sky.

Students write answers to all three Let us Think A questions in their notebooks individually, using complete sentences. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are unsure with a line reference from the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together, students already carry the imagery in their ears — use that familiarity to anchor comprehension: ask them to close their eyes and picture what the poet sees before they answer question 1. Question 3 ('why the air is blue') has no single correct answer; accept any reasoned response that refers to the sky.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Rhyme and Personal Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.104): paired discussion — swings seen, what students would like to see from a swing.
Let us Listen (p.107): listen to the poem, list rhyming pairs, add two more rhyming words of own choice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud from p.103 at a steady pace — this is the listening round for Let us Listen (p.107). Students keep books closed and simply listen.
Teacher reads the poem a second time, more slowly. Students listen again and this time quietly note any word pairs that sound alike at the end of lines.

Let us Listen (p.107) — pairs compare their lists of rhyming pairs, then share with the class. Teacher builds a class list on the board: swing–thing, blue–do, wall–all, wide–countryside, green–seen, brown–down. Each pair also contributes two rhyming words of their own choice and explains why the pair rhymes.

Let us Think B (p.104) — guided conversation in pairs, then whole-class share. Question 1: Where have you seen a swing? What was it made of? Question 2: What would you like to see from high up on a swing? Teacher draws out vivid, imaginative responses and writes a few striking images on the board.
Three or four volunteers share their imagined aerial view to the class in two or three sentences each. Class votes (thumbs up/thumbs down) on which imagined view sounded most vivid or surprising.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task requires the teacher to read the poem aloud clearly from p.103 — read at a pace slow enough for students to isolate line-end sounds. When students add their own rhyming pairs, accept any genuine rhyme (not just poem vocabulary) to encourage creative engagement with sound.

periods.activity_title: Verbs and Nouns: One Word, Two Jobs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns (pp.105–106): identify verb and noun uses of dance, play, answer, fly, waves in sentence pairs.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn — Stringing Together (p.104): write one set of five expanding sentences, each longer than the last.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the sentence pair from the poem on the board: 'I swing on a swing.' Students identify which 'swing' is doing something (verb) and which 'swing' is a thing (noun). Teacher explains briefly that many words serve both roles depending on their position in a sentence.

Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns (p.105): teacher reads the 'dance' and 'play' sentence pairs aloud. Students circle the verb and underline the noun on mini whiteboards or in their notebooks. Whole-class check after each pair before moving on.

Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns (p.106): teacher reads the 'answer', 'fly', and 'waves' sentence pairs. Students work independently to circle the verb and underline the noun for each pair, then compare with a partner.

Whole-class review of all five pairs. For each one, a student volunteers the answer and explains in one sentence HOW they knew which role the word was playing (position, meaning, what follows the word). Teacher corrects gently and consolidates the rule: the same word can be a verb or a noun — context decides.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may find 'waves' the trickiest pair because both uses carry a plural ending — draw attention to the subject and what the word is doing in each sentence to resolve the ambiguity. The homework task on sentence expansion can be completed independently; it requires only a blank page and the model example on p.104.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.107): tongue twister and /W/ phonics drill with lip-shape practice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the /W/ sound: demonstrate making an 'O' shape with the lips and producing the /W/ before releasing it into a word — 'win', 'wait', 'white'. Students mirror the lip shape in pairs.

Let us Speak (p.107) — tongue twister round. Teacher models 'How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?' slowly, then at normal pace. Students repeat chorally four to five times, gradually picking up speed while keeping the lip shape consistent.

Let us Speak (p.107) — word-list drill. Teacher reads each word from the list (fever, fewer, valley, white, vine, wise, win, wait, vet, wet) and students echo with the correct lip shape. Students then sort the words with a partner: 'Which words have the /W/ sound? Which do not?' (fever, valley, vet do not.)

Individual performance round: each student reads the word list aloud once at their seat while teacher circulates and notes who is confusing /V/ and /W/. Two volunteers attempt the tongue twister solo for the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The key confusion at this level is /V/ versus /W/ — 'vine' versus 'win', 'vet' versus 'wet'. The sorting activity in the middle of the unit surfaces this contrast explicitly. If students struggle with the tongue twister at speed, slow it down and build pace gradually rather than rushing to fluency.

periods.activity_title: Modelled Writing: A Paragraph About Free-Time Activities

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write 1 (p.108): write a short paragraph about activities enjoyed in free time.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the word 'pleasantest' from the poem: the poet says swinging is the pleasantest thing a child can do. Students brainstorm aloud: what is the pleasantest thing THEY enjoy doing? Teacher lists five or six responses on the board as a word bank.

Modelled writing (p.108) — teacher thinks aloud while composing a sample paragraph on the board: topic sentence, two or three activity sentences with simple reasons, closing sentence. Students watch the process of choosing words and arranging ideas before any writing of their own.

Let us Write 1 (p.108) — students plan their own paragraph by jotting two or three activities in bullet form first, then draft the full paragraph in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and prompts with questions ('Why do you enjoy it? When do you do it?') to help students add detail.

Two or three volunteers read their paragraphs aloud. Class listens and identifies the topic sentence in each. Teacher offers brief whole-class feedback on one strength and one suggestion noticed across the drafts.

periods.teacher_notes: The model paragraph on the board is the scaffold — keep it visible while students draft so they can borrow its structure without copying its content. Encourage students to use at least one word from the poem's vocabulary (pleasantest, wide, countryside) if they can weave it in naturally.

periods.activity_title: Prepositions in Context: Garden Picture Fill-In

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write 2 (p.109): fill in blanks with prepositions from the box using the garden illustration.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the seven prepositions from the box (on, beside, between, above, in front of, behind, under) using a quick classroom demonstration — place a pencil on, under, beside and behind a book and ask students to call out the correct word each time.

Students open to p.109 and examine the garden illustration carefully. Teacher leads a picture walk: 'What do you see? Where is the ladybug? Where is the watercan?' Students respond orally with full sentences before writing anything.

Let us Write 2 (p.109) — students fill in all seven blanks independently using the preposition box and the picture as guides. Teacher moves through the class and redirects any student who is guessing without looking at the picture.

Whole-class correction: teacher reads each sentence aloud and students call out their answer. Teacher writes the correct preposition for each blank on the board and briefly explains any item where responses were split.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture on p.109 is the primary reference for every answer — remind students to look at the image, not to guess. 'Between' (ladybug between two pots) and 'in front of' (watercan in front of the pots) are the two most commonly confused items at this level; pause slightly longer on both during whole-class correction.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — Stringing Together (p.104): frame a set of expanding sentences, each longer than the last.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the model expansion on p.104 aloud step by step — from 'Jeevan waited.' all the way to the five-part sentence — pausing after each addition to ask: 'What new information did we just add? Where does it fit?'

Whole-class guided practice: teacher writes 'Meena laughed.' on the board and the class collectively builds it up in four or five steps, with students suggesting each addition and the teacher scribing. The class decides after each step whether the sentence still makes sense.

Let us Learn (p.104) — students choose their own simple starting sentence (two or three words) and write a set of five expanding sentences independently in their notebooks, each longer than the previous. Teacher circulates and nudges students who are adding random words rather than meaningful detail.
Three volunteers read their expansion chains aloud — the class hears the sentence grow with each reading. The class identifies what type of information was added at each step (when, where, why, how).

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with verb/noun pairs earlier in the chapter, students can now bring that vocabulary into expanded sentences — encourage them to use a word they know both as a verb and a noun somewhere in their chain if possible. The key error to watch is students adding length without adding meaning; the oral class-building step exposes this pattern before individual writing.

periods.activity_title: Swings of Imagination: Draw and Write

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.110): draw a magical swing, then write a short adventure paragraph.

time_bands.activity: Teacher prompts imagination: 'Stevenson's swing took him above walls and countryside. If YOUR swing could take you anywhere — outer space, a jungle, a world inside a book — where would it go?' Students share ideas briefly with a partner.

Let us Do (p.110) — drawing phase. Students draw their magical swing and its destination on a fresh page. Teacher encourages labelling the key elements in the drawing (the destination, two or three things visible from the swing).

Writing phase: students write a short paragraph (four to six sentences) about the adventure their magical swing takes them on — where it goes, what they see, and how it feels. The drawing stays visible beside the writing as a reference.

Gallery walk: students place their work on their desks and the class walks around quietly for a few minutes. Each student leaves a small sticky-note or writes one word of appreciation on a slip beside a piece that struck them.

periods.teacher_notes: The joy of the poem's imagery — rivers, trees, cattle, a green garden seen from above — is the launchpad for imagination here; students who feel stuck can be reminded of those images and asked to replace the countryside with their own chosen world. Keep the drawing and writing together in one sitting so neither depends on the other being done earlier.

periods.activity_title: Swings Across Festivals: Explore and Share

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p.110): find out which festivals or months are linked to swinging; collect and share with class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the exploration by asking: 'Has anyone sat on a swing during a festival or a special time of year?' Students share memories briefly. Teacher notes any festivals mentioned on the board.

Let us Explore (p.110) — teacher provides a short prepared fact-sheet or speaks from notes: Teej (Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh) and Hariyali Teej involve decorated swings; Dol Purnima (Bengal) features swings for Krishna's idol; the monsoon months are traditionally associated with outdoor swinging in many Indian states. Students note key facts in two or three lines.

In groups of three or four, students combine their notes and prepare a short oral report (three to four sentences) to share with the class: which festival or month, where in India, and what the swinging means or looks like. Teacher circulates and helps each group shape their sentences.

Each group delivers their oral report. After all groups have shared, the class identifies which region of India had the most mentions and whether any festival appears on more than one group's list — a brief collective summary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have personal experience of festival swinging are a rich resource — invite them to describe what the swing looked like or felt like, connecting lived knowledge to the poem's imagery of joy and height. If the fact-sheet is not available, the teacher's own knowledge of two or three festivals is sufficient to ground the exploration.

time_bands.activity: Whole-class recitation of 'The Swing' (p.103) from memory — students who remember the full poem recite it; others join in on the lines they know. The aim is a joyful, confident group performance that shows how far their command of the poem has grown.

Rapid-fire review game: teacher calls out a concept from the chapter and students respond on mini boards or by raising hands. Round 1 — rhyming pairs from the poem. Round 2 — one word used as both a verb and a noun (students give a sentence for each use). Round 3 — a preposition that fits a given scenario ('The cat is ___ the table'). This weaves sound-work, grammar, and language use into a single playful sweep.

Students write a four-line poem or a four-sentence paragraph in their notebooks: either a mini-poem imagining their own swing ride inspired by Stevenson's images of the open air and wide countryside, OR a paragraph connecting the poem's theme of childhood freedom to a festival or season they know involves swinging. Students choose their own form — no scaffolding is provided.

Volunteers read their compositions aloud. After each reading the class identifies: one image or word they liked, and whether the piece captured the feeling of freedom that runs through 'The Swing'. Teacher highlights two or three strong choices of language across the readings.

Closing choral recitation of the final stanza of 'The Swing' — 'Till I look down on the garden green…'. Teacher invites the class to think of one word that captures what the chapter gave them. A few words are called out and the teacher writes them on the board as a simple closing word-cloud.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws together the rhyme and rhythm of the poem, the verb/noun and preposition work, the imaginative writing, and the cultural exploration — students should feel the chapter as a whole rather than as separate activities. The choice between the mini-poem and the paragraph in the writing phase honours different strengths; both are legitimate responses to the chapter.
materials: Mini whiteboards or slips of paper

items.item_stem: When the swing goes over the wall, the poet sees a wide landscape. Which of the following correctly lists what the poet sees?

options.label: A
options.text: A green garden, a brown roof, and the sky only.

options.label: B
options.text: Fields, flowers, birds, and a river.

options.label: C
options.text: Mountains, lakes, horses, and the ocean.

options.label: D
options.text: Rivers, trees, cattle, and the countryside.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be recalling familiar landscape words rather than attending to the poem's specific details.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has drawn on general nature vocabulary instead of the poem's actual second stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused the third stanza's downward-glance images with the broader landscape seen from above the wall.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 103 beginning “Oh, I do think it the pleasantest thing.” In your own words, explain what the poet feels about swinging, and say why you think the poet calls the air ‘blue’ rather than using a different description.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The poet feels that swinging is the most enjoyable thing a child can do, and the joy is shown in the enthusiastic opening exclamation. The air is called blue to paint the wide, open sky the child sees while swinging upward — it suggests brightness, freedom, and the feeling of being up high under an open sky.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read aloud the first two stanzas of 'The Swing' (Textbook p.103). Listen carefully, then answer: which two words at the ends of lines in the first stanza rhyme with each other?

options.text: In the first stanza, 'blue' and 'wall' rhyme.
In the first stanza, 'swing' and 'thing' rhyme.
In the second stanza, 'wall' and 'blue' rhyme.
In the second stanza, 'wide' and 'countryside' rhyme.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 — True: 'swing' and 'thing' are the end-words of lines 1 and 3 of the first stanza and rhyme. Statement 2 — False: 'blue' rhymes with 'do', not with 'wall'. Statement 3 — True: 'wide' and 'countryside' are the end-words of lines 2 and 4 of the second stanza and rhyme. Statement 4 — False: 'wall' rhymes with 'all', not with 'blue'.

items.item_stem: Recite any one complete stanza of 'The Swing' from memory. Then tell the class: if YOU were on a swing rising high into the air, what one thing would you most want to see below you — and why?

expected_elements: Recites a full stanza with correct words.
Names a specific thing they would see.
Gives a reason for their choice.

items.item_stem:
Look at the picture on Textbook page 109 showing the garden scene. Fill in each blank with the correct preposition from the box: on, beside, between, above, in front of, behind, under.
1. There is a ladybug ________ the two flower pots.
2. A butterfly is flying ________ the flower.
3. The watercan is ________ the flower pots.
4. An ant is walking ________ the leaf.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. between  2. above  3. in front of  4. under

items.item_stem: Robert Louis Stevenson's poet finds swinging the most enjoyable thing a child can do. Write a short paragraph of four to six sentences about the activities YOU enjoy most in your free time. Use at least two of these prepositions naturally in your paragraph: on, beside, above, under, behind.

expected_elements: Names two or more specific free-time activities.
Uses at least two prepositions correctly in sentences.
Writes in complete sentences with a clear topic.

items.item_stem: Each sentence below uses a word that can be either a verb or a noun. Match each sentence to the correct label.
items.visual_stimulus:
Sentence | Verb or Noun?
The play begins at six o'clock. | ?
I like to play in the garden. | ?
There is a fly on the window. | ?
Birds fly over the rooftop. | ?

answer_key.left: The play begins at six o'clock.
I like to play in the garden.
There is a fly on the window.

items.item_stem: The word 'swing' in the poem is used as a noun — it names the object the child sits on. Write TWO sentences of your own using the word 'swing': one sentence where it is a NOUN and one where it is a VERB.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Noun example: The swing in our garden is made of rope and a wooden plank. Verb example: I swing back and forth until I can see over the wall.

items.item_stem: Stevenson's swing took the poet above walls and over the countryside. Imagine a magical swing that can carry you to one place of your choice — anywhere in the world or beyond. Draw the swing and its destination, then write four to six sentences describing what you see and feel during the ride. Share your drawing and description with the class.

expected_elements: Drawing shows a swing and a clearly imagined destination.
Writing describes what is seen or felt on the ride.
Oral share is clear and confident to the class.
